newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian welfare talks win union vote of confidence.
newsitem.headline: Italian welfare talks win union vote of confidence.

text.p: Italian union leaders said on Tuesday they were hopeful a much-sought agreement on welfare reform could be reached by the autumn, but employers warned that time was running out to forge a worthwhile deal.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi launched the welfare review in mid-June and government, unions and employers held their last round of talks before the summer break on Tuesday.
Negotiations are due to start again on August 28, with Prodi looking to strike a deal by the end of September.

"We have noticed a step forward in our negotiations. It is possible that the resumption of talks will lead to a solution that will have our consent," Sergio Cofferati, the head of Italy's largest union, told reporters.
Prodi said he was "by and large satisfied" with how the talks had progressed since their start.
"These were weeks of intense and productive meetings which pinpointed existing problems and areas that need reform."

But employers federation Confindustria warned that no firm decisions had been taken on how to reduce social spending, which economists say allots too much money to the pensions system while offering little help to the unemployed or young families.
"We are basically at the same point we were a month ago," Confindustria chairman Giorgio Fossa said after the meeting.

The government is under pressure to enact a thorough welfare reform to prove that state finances can be kept under control following the planned launch of the single European currency in 1999 and hopes to include the changes in its 1998 budget.
The budget must be presented to parliament by the end of September.
"We have lost almost a month and a half. If we don't define measures by September 15, we will definitively have lost hope," Fossa said.
Reforming Italy's cash-guzzling pension system, which is the thorniest issue of the negotiations, will be addressed on the first day the talks resume next month.

The government is trying to slash its pension bill by some five trillion lire ($2.8 billion) and is looking to phase out the current system whereby pensions are calculated according to how long a person has worked.
Instead, the government wants to introduce a system based solely on contributions workers have paid into pension funds.
But pension cuts are deeply opposed by the hard-left Communist Refoundation party whose support gives Prodi a majority in parliament and by several union members.

Labour union optimism on pension reform grew last week when the government said it was willing to separate reform of pension spending from that of other issues, such as health care and unemployment benefits.
Cofferati said on Tuesday the unions expect "a careful verification" of the pension system. "It will then be our job, with the government, to introduce the necessary corrections."
Unions are also confident that Prodi plans to include measures to boost employment as part of the welfare reform.
But the leader of the Cisl union, Sergio D'Antoni, cautioned on Tuesday that so far the government's initiatives on employment were just a "list of good intentions".
Another reform that both unions and employers agreed needed to be tackled in September was curbing Italy's widespread tax evasion.
